To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Rho is activated at the onset of cytokinesis, that Rho is rapidly inactivated at the end of cytokinesis, but that inactivation of RHO is not necessary for cytokinesis to be completed.
Rho undergoes a rapid cycle of activation/inactivation during cytokinesis and that this cycle is necessary for cytokinesis to proceed.

Rho GTP hydrolysis is required throughout the duration of cytokinesis, but that the rate of GTP hydrolyses is controlled by the cytokinectic apparatus, which in turn is controlled by the rate of GEF and GAP activities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of Rho and the Rho GEFs in cytokinesis, and with the role of Rac and the Rho GAPs in the regulation of the actin cytoskeleton.
the control and regulation of the small GTPases and how this control is important for cytokinesis.
how the Rho G-proteins are controlled and the implications of their control for the cell.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cytokinetic machinery is controlled by flux of Rho GTP binding proteins.
cytokinesis is controlled by the flux of Rho GTP binding proteins.
the Rho G-protein cycle is a critical component of cytokinesis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the flux of the RHo GTPases through the GTP/GDP cycle is required for proper cytokinete apparatus function.
the cytokinetic machinery is controlled not by Rho, per se, but rather by the flux through Rho, i.e. the rate at which Rho cycles between active and inactive states.
the Rho GEFs and GTPase activating proteins (GAPs) are the major regulators of the GTPase activity of Rho, Rac and Cdc-42.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the flux through the GTP/GDP cycle is a critical feature of Rho GTP binding and hydrolysis, and is necessary for proper function of the Rho family GTPases.
the Rho GEF and GAP activities that control the GTPase cycling of Rho are not simply required to activate or inactivate Rho, but rather, to maintain the flux of Rho through the GTP and GDP states.
Rho GTP binding and GTP hydrolysis are tightly coupled, such that the flux of Rho through the GTP cycle is essential for cytokinetic apparatus formation and function.
